newsitem.title: TAIWAN: GE turns up heat in Taiwan nuclear plant showdown.
newsitem.headline: GE turns up heat in Taiwan nuclear plant showdown.

text.p: U.S. contractor General Electric Co (GE) turned up the heat in a political showdown over Taiwan's fourth nuclear power station, indicating it would seek compensation if construction were delayed beyond Wednesday.
GE served notice on state utility Taiwan Power Co (Taipower) that it would not extend a midnight (1600 GMT) deadline for starting work on the stalled project, Taipower officials said.
"General Electric has given Taiwan Power a written notice stating its decision not to extend the deadline," utility vice president Lin Chin-chi told Reuters by telephone.
"This means GE would be able to seek compensation if parliament does not agree to support the project by midnight tonight," Lin said.

Despite GE's deadline, the fate of the US$4.1 billion power plant -- and GE's US$1.8 billion contract to supply its twin reactors and generators -- remained undecided pending a final vote in parliament scheduled for Friday.

Parliament embarrassed Taipei in May by cancelling funds for the project, but the government and Taipower have pushed ahead anyway, filing an appeal to parliament in June. Opponents can make the cancellation stand only with a two-thirds vote of parliament.

The outcome is far from certain. The ruling Nationalist Party's legislative branch proposed on Wednesday to delay work on the highly controversial project for two more months to build political consensus.
"We hope to handle the case until we reach some sort of consensus," parliament speaker Liu Sung-fan told reporters after a ruling party meeting.
The executive branch is reluctant to back down.
"We do not know the exact details (of the legislative branch proposal)," vice premier Hsu Li-teh told reporters. "We will need to carefully study related technical problems."

Economics vice-minister Chang Chang-pang told the mass circulation China Times that Taipei had already evaluated the nuclear project for more than 10 years, implying a further review was redundant and unnecessary.

Parliamentary debate was set for Tuesday but opposition Democratic Progressive Party lawmakers blocked any action by physically barring Premier Lien Chan from the building to explain the cabinet's appeal and defend the project.
Taipower, which has continued with work despite the deadlock, asked GE in September to start work.
The utility has already sunk US$220 million into preliminary work on the 2,700-megawatt nuclear power station.
Taipower's Lin would not estimate how much GE might seek in compensation if the project is delayed beyond the contractual deadline, calling this a matter for the courts.
GE officials in Taipei declined to comment on the notice.
Premier Lien, visibly angered by Tuesday's rebuff, said the move represented a "dark day" for Taiwan's fledgling democracy and denounced the use of force rather than reason.
Media commentaries criticised the handling of the matter.
"Why can't we sit down and calmly discuss the fourth nuclear power project?" a China Times' commentator asked.

The United Daily News said: "The nuclear debate has become an issue of politics. It has nothing to do with right and wrong. Nobody really cares about the law and justice and nobody cares about the dignity of the constitution."

Taiwan approved the plant in 1994 after years of delays and protests sparked by the 1986 Chernobyl disaster in the Soviet Union. A growing number of opponents in increasingly democratic Taiwan say nuclear power is dangerous and unnecessary.
